title: 1 Peter
summary: First Peter is a Greek letter from "Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ" to elect sojourners across five Roman provinces of Asia Minor. It joins new birth and living hope, holiness, people-of-God identity, honorable public conduct, household exhortation, suffering, baptism, gifts, eldership, humility, and resistance while leaving authorship, date, Babylon, audience profile, and the scale of hostility disputed.
historical_context: The prescript addresses elect sojourners of the diaspora in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia; the closing names Silvanus, Mark, and "Babylon." Rome is the dominant interpretation of Babylon, but the letter does not say Rome. Proposals range from direct Petrine authorship with secretarial or collaborative assistance to composition in Peter's name after his death. Insults, slander, social alienation, and threatened or actual suffering are explicit; a coordinated empire-wide persecution or one legal proceeding is not.
ancient_near_east_context: First Peter is a first-century eastern Mediterranean text, not an ancient Near Eastern composition. Israelite exodus, holiness, priesthood, exile, Noah, Zion, and suffering-righteous traditions in the Hebrew Bible are textual antecedents; comparison with earlier Levantine temple and royal practices must be mediated through those scriptures and later Jewish reception.
hebraic_worldview: First Peter reasons extensively with Israel's scriptures and identity language: election, holiness, exodus-like ransom, covenant people, priesthood, sacrifice, exile, Zion, Noah, blessing, judgment, and shepherding. These appropriations require Jewish-contextual reading and must not become antisemitic replacement claims.
second_temple_context: Second Temple Jewish election, diaspora, exile, temple, priesthood, sacrifice, apocalyptic judgment, angelic and spirit traditions, and scriptural interpretation illuminate the letter. Such comparanda do not prove one sectarian source, an exclusively Jewish audience, or direct literary dependence.
canonical_context: Within the Catholic or General Epistles, First Peter rereads Torah, Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Hosea, and the Noah tradition around Messiah's suffering, resurrection, communal holiness, and hope. Comparisons with Pauline letters and Acts are valuable, but shared names and themes do not settle authorship, chronology, or dependence.
later_christian_reception: Reception broadly associated the letter with the apostle Peter and interpreted Babylon as Rome. The letter has sustained theology of baptism, atonement, descent to the dead, priesthood, church, suffering, ministry, and household order; it has also been misused to legitimate slavery, abusive submission, political quietism, and suffering glorification.
literary_context: The work opens and closes as a diaspora letter, while its sustained blessing, scriptural catenae, household exhortations, baptismal language, suffering rhetoric, and elder address have generated proposals involving homily, baptismal tradition, liturgy, paraenesis, and testament. These proposed sources or forms do not require partition of the received letter.
covenantal_significance: Election, holiness, covenant-people language, priesthood, mercy, and scriptural promise are applied to the addressees through Messiah. Christian theological use must acknowledge the letter's Jewish scriptural reasoning and avoid claiming that God rejected or replaced Jewish people.
authorship_positions: Traditional and some modern interpreters identify the named sender with Peter the apostle, sometimes proposing Silvanus as secretary, courier, collaborator, or stylistic mediator.

Other scholars argue that language, social setting, reception, and the letter's relation to Pauline traditions favor a later author writing in Peter's name; ethical evaluation of ancient pseudepigraphy is separately debated.

The closing says the author wrote "through Silvanus" and sends greetings from "Babylon" with Mark; neither phrase discloses a complete production process, and Babylon is commonly read as Rome without being explicitly equated with Rome.
date_ranges: Direct Petrine proposals commonly place composition in the early or mid-60s CE, before Peter's traditional death under Nero.
Post-Petrine proposals commonly place composition approximately 70-95 CE, with some ranges extending wider.
No named ruler, war, destruction of Jerusalem, or datable persecution fixes an absolute date.
original_audience: The addressees are explicitly distributed across five Roman provinces and styled elect sojourners of diaspora. Israel-shaped language, former ignorance, ancestral way of life, and former gentile conduct are weighed differently; Jewish, gentile, and mixed reconstructions remain in debate, and the letter does not provide a demographic census.
historical_setting: The letter does not identify a named emperor, province-wide prosecution, destination city, itinerary, or complete community network. It depicts dispersed assemblies facing slander, estrangement, and suffering, with enslaved household members, wives, husbands, elders, younger people, rulers, masters, outsiders, and gifted speakers and servants.
canonical_role: First Peter gives a compact canonical synthesis of living hope, holiness, scripturally formed communal identity, public conduct, suffering with Christ, baptism, mutual service, accountable shepherding, humility, vigilance, and grace.

new_testament_connections: Pauline blessing, household, suffering, gift, and body-of-Messiah language provide comparanda without proving literary dependence.
Acts supplies a later narrative portrait of Peter, Silas, Mark, and Roman mission but cannot fill the letter's silences.
Jude and Second Peter are important textual and collection comparanda, especially in Papyrus 72.
Revelation uses Babylon explicitly for an imperial city, strengthening but not proving the same identification in First Peter.

claims.claim: The prescript names Peter as an apostle of Jesus Christ.
claims.rationale: The claim directly reflects the preserved prescript.

claims.claim: The addressees are styled elect sojourners of diaspora in five named provinces.
claims.rationale: The wording is explicit while the social force of sojourner and diaspora is disputed.

claims.claim: Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia are named in the address.
claims.rationale: The provincial list is explicit.

claims.claim: The opening blessing connects new birth into living hope with Jesus Christ's resurrection.
claims.rationale: The connection is grammatical and explicit.

claims.claim: The addressees are commanded to be holy with a citation of scriptural holiness language.
claims.rationale: The imperative and scriptural wording are explicit.

claims.claim: The letter contrasts inherited futile conduct with ransom by Christ's precious blood.
claims.rationale: The imagery is explicit while atonement models differ.

claims.claim: New birth is associated with imperishable seed through God's living and enduring word.
claims.rationale: The association is explicit while seed and word metaphors admit differing nuances.

claims.claim: Christ is presented as a living stone and the addressees as living stones being built into a spiritual house.
claims.rationale: The imagery is explicit while ecclesiological extension differs.

claims.claim: The addressees receive royal-priesthood and holy-nation language drawn from Israel's scriptures.
claims.rationale: The scriptural appropriation is explicit; replacement interpretations are contested.

claims.claim: Honorable conduct among the nations is linked to responding to slander and anticipated divine visitation.
claims.rationale: The rhetorical link is explicit while the visitation phrase is disputed.

claims.claim: The letter calls for submission to human institutions while also commanding fear of God.
claims.rationale: Both commands occur in the unit; their political scope is debated.

claims.claim: The household address directly exhorts enslaved household members under masters, including unjust masters.
claims.rationale: The ancient status and asymmetry are explicit and ethically contested in reception.

claims.claim: Christ's suffering is presented both as an example to follow and in sin-bearing and healing imagery.
claims.rationale: Both rhetorical functions appear; later atonement syntheses vary.

claims.claim: Wives and husbands are separately addressed within an unequal Greco-Roman household setting.
claims.rationale: The addresses and asymmetry are textual; normative extension is disputed.

claims.claim: The addressees are told not to repay evil or abuse in kind but to bless.
claims.rationale: The contrast is explicit.

claims.claim: The letter calls for a prepared answer concerning hope, given with gentleness and respect and a good conscience.
claims.rationale: The manner and object of the answer are explicit.

claims.claim: The received text says Christ made proclamation to spirits in prison who were disobedient in Noah's days.
claims.rationale: The wording is preserved while agent, time, location, and audience of proclamation are disputed.

claims.claim: The Noah-water comparison is followed by the statement that a corresponding antitype, baptism, now saves.
claims.rationale: The statement is explicit while sacramental explanations differ.

claims.claim: The letter says good news was proclaimed even to the dead, without identifying them or the time of proclamation.
claims.rationale: The statement is explicit but its referents and chronology are not.

claims.claim: Eschatological exhortation joins prayer, persistent love, hospitality, and stewarding gifts in speech and service.
claims.rationale: The practices form one explicit exhortative unit.

claims.claim: The addressees are told not to regard the fiery trial as strange and to distinguish suffering as Christians from suffering for wrongdoing.
claims.rationale: The contrast is explicit while the historical form of trial is uncertain.

claims.claim: The letter says it is time for judgment to begin from God's household.
claims.rationale: The wording is explicit while the judgment's nature and sequence are debated.

claims.claim: Elders are exhorted to shepherd willingly and eagerly without domination, as examples to the flock.
claims.rationale: The leadership constraints are explicit; later polity differs.

claims.claim: Humility, mutual relation, and casting anxiety on God form the transition into vigilance.
claims.rationale: The sequence is explicit while the submission syntax is discussed.

claims.claim: The adversary, the devil, is compared to a roaring lion seeking someone to devour.
claims.rationale: The simile is explicit while metaphysical and pastoral extensions vary.

claims.claim: The closing names Silvanus, Babylon, and Mark but does not define their full identities or roles.
claims.rationale: The names are explicit; identification and reconstruction require external evidence.

claims.claim: The prescript's Petrine attribution does not by itself resolve whether Peter composed the received Greek letter directly, through collaboration, or not at all.
claims.rationale: Internal attribution, production mechanisms, and historical authorship are related but distinct questions.

claims.claim: First Peter contains no named event that fixes an absolute composition date.
claims.rationale: Published dates depend on authorship, Babylon, suffering, and reception arguments.

claims.claim: Rome is a probable symbolic identification of Babylon, but First Peter never explicitly says that Babylon means Rome.
claims.rationale: Early reception and imperial symbolism favor Rome while the equation remains inferential.

claims.claim: The letter's language supports debate over Jewish, gentile, and mixed recipients but does not settle exact demographics.
claims.rationale: Different textual indicators point in more than one direction.

claims.claim: First Peter attests social hostility and suffering but does not name Nero, Domitian, Trajan, or an empire-wide persecution decree.
claims.rationale: Hostility is explicit while institutional scale and chronology are not.

claims.claim: First Peter is a coherent letter employing blessing, paraenesis, scriptural interpretation, household discourse, and apocalyptic consolation.
claims.rationale: The received form is epistolary; source and form-critical reconstructions remain debated.

interpretive_notes.note: Authorship remains disputed: the prescript names Peter, but language, historical setting, reception, collaboration, secretary, and pseudepigraphy proposals are weighed differently.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Attribution and historical production are not identical questions.

interpretive_notes.note: Silvanus may be courier, secretary, collaborator, stylistic mediator, or the person through whom the letter was sent; dia Silouanou does not settle his role.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The preposition and sparse notice underdetermine production history.

interpretive_notes.note: Babylon probably signifies Rome in view of early reception and imperial symbolism, but literal Babylon and other proposals remain possible and the letter never supplies the equation.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The dominant inference is not explicit identification.

interpretive_notes.note: The date cannot be fixed from a named event; early and later ranges depend on authorship, Babylon, suffering, and reception arguments.
interpretive_notes.rationale: No ruler or datable crisis is named.

interpretive_notes.note: The five-province circuit is explicit, but it does not identify destination cities, the route of delivery, or a unified provincial organization.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Administrative names do not supply a complete itinerary.

interpretive_notes.note: Elect sojourners of diaspora can combine geographic dispersion, marginal social identity, and Israel-shaped theological rhetoric; no one gloss proves ethnicity or legal status.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The linked terms have overlapping literal and metaphorical uses.

interpretive_notes.note: Former ignorance, ancestral conduct, and former gentile excess favor substantial gentile presence, while Israel's scriptural address and possible Jewish recipients prevent demographic certainty.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The audience evidence is cumulative but incomplete.

interpretive_notes.note: Foreknowledge appears in the prescript's triadic description; later predestination systems must be labeled as theological reception rather than smuggled into the lexical item.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Literary function and systematic models are distinct layers.

interpretive_notes.note: New birth, living hope, inheritance, and resurrection form one blessing; the imagery promises durable belonging without making present suffering unreal.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The unit coordinates hope and grief in trials.

interpretive_notes.note: Testing faith by fire is a refining metaphor and must not be used to glorify trauma, manufacture persecution, discourage safety, or blame victims for insufficient faith.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Metaphorical testing does not authorize causing or prolonging harm.

interpretive_notes.note: Be holy cites Israel's scripture and calls for whole conduct before God; it cannot justify purity-culture shame, misogyny, anti-LGBTQ coercion, ableism, or exclusion from care.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Scriptural holiness must be interpreted without dehumanizing applications.

interpretive_notes.note: Ransom and blood language evokes costly liberation and sacrificial imagery; competing atonement models should not be collapsed into a single lexical claim or used to glorify violence.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Image and later doctrinal synthesis are distinct.

interpretive_notes.note: Imperishable seed and enduring word explain communal new birth; biological, racial, or nationalist readings contradict the rhetorical contrast with perishable life.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The metaphor concerns divine agency and durable proclamation, not ancestry.

interpretive_notes.note: Logikon milk may mean rational, spiritual, or word-related nourishment; translation cannot establish a sacramental or anti-intellectual theory by itself.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The adjective has a debated semantic range.

interpretive_notes.note: Living stones and spiritual house are communal temple metaphors centered on the scriptural cornerstone; they do not identify a building, clerical caste, or territorial Christian state.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Metaphorical corporate identity differs from later institutional claims.

interpretive_notes.note: People of God and royal priesthood language must not become antisemitism, supersessionism, ethnic nationalism, or a claim that Jewish people were rejected; First Peter reasons through Israel's scriptures rather than erasing Israel.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Responsible reception distinguishes Christian appropriation from anti-Jewish replacement.

interpretive_notes.note: Honorable conduct responds to slander through visible good works; it does not require assimilation, respectability politics, concealment of abuse, or silence before injustice.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Witness language cannot erase truth-telling or protection.

interpretive_notes.note: Submission to authorities is bounded in the same paragraph by freedom, universal honor, sibling love, fear of God, and limited honor of the emperor; it is not unlimited obedience.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The coordinated imperatives resist absolutizing one command.

interpretive_notes.note: Authorities language must not legitimate authoritarian government, nationalism, colonial rule, concealment of state violence, or obedience to commands that produce injustice and harm.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Ancient accommodation is not a blank check for modern power.

interpretive_notes.note: Slavery is an exploitative status relation in the passage, not benign employment; the exhortation must never support slavery apologetics, trafficking, returning people to enslavers, or worker exploitation.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Historical naming and ethical reception must center the enslaved and reject ownership of persons.

interpretive_notes.note: Christ's footsteps address unjust suffering in an enslaved-person unit; imitation cannot mean seeking harm, staying with an abuser, refusing rescue, or shielding perpetrators from accountability.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Nonretaliation and access to safety and justice are compatible.

interpretive_notes.note: Sin-bearing, wounds, healing, shepherd, and guardian images combine scriptural and pastoral language; later atonement theories must identify their additional synthesis.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The unit's images are explicit but not a complete systematic model.

interpretive_notes.note: Household submission operates inside ancient patriarchal asymmetry; the unit also addresses husbands as responsible for knowledge and honor and warns that abuse of power disrupts prayer.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Historical household structure and the letter's internal counterpressures must both be seen.

interpretive_notes.note: Household exhortation must not authorize domestic abuse, coercive submission, marital rape, forced marriage, victim blaming, or pressure to remain in danger; safety and accountability take priority.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Ancient accommodation cannot override consent or bodily safety.

interpretive_notes.note: Sarah's obedience and lord language belong to scriptural reception and household rhetoric; they do not make all women daughters only through deference to men or establish male superiority.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The example's scope and normative force are contested.

interpretive_notes.note: Repaying evil with blessing refuses retaliatory harm; it does not prohibit boundaries, truthful reporting, legal protection, communal discipline, or solidarity with victims.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Nonretaliation is not non-accountability.

interpretive_notes.note: The requested defense concerns hope and must be offered with gentleness and respect; the verse cannot license aggressive apologetics, harassment, forced conversion, or contempt for other religions.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The manner of witness is part of the command.

interpretive_notes.note: In 3:18, Christ may be put to death in flesh and made alive in spirit, by the Spirit, or in contrasting modes of existence; grammar and theology remain disputed.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Dative syntax and the next clause support competing readings.

interpretive_notes.note: Spirits in prison have been read as fallen angels, dead humans from Noah's generation, or other spiritual beings; proclamation may announce victory, judgment, or good news, and no option is textually effortless.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Second Temple spirit traditions and grammar permit multiple reconstructions.

interpretive_notes.note: The spirits passage must not generate occult speculation, coercive deliverance practices, diagnoses of mental illness as possession, or dangerous exorcism.
interpretive_notes.rationale: An obscure ancient claim cannot override medical care, consent, and safety.

interpretive_notes.note: Noah's eight persons were brought safely through water, while the antitype is carefully distinguished from removing bodily dirt and related to conscience or appeal and resurrection.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The explanatory qualifications belong to the baptism statement.

interpretive_notes.note: Baptism now saves has generated sacramental, covenantal, symbolic, and faith-response accounts; it must not support forced baptism, magical guarantees, or denial of grace to people unable to receive a rite.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The wording is strong and its qualifying clauses are equally important.

interpretive_notes.note: Proclamation to the dead in 4:6 may concern believers who later died, the generally dead, or a descent-related group; relation to 3:19 is debated.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Referent and chronology are not supplied.

interpretive_notes.note: Love covers a multitude of sins evokes wisdom tradition and communal forbearance; it cannot mean hiding abuse, destroying evidence, silencing survivors, or avoiding safeguarding reports.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Forgiving love and institutional concealment are morally distinct.

interpretive_notes.note: Hospitality and gifts are reciprocal stewardship, not tools for patronage control, prosperity extraction, unpaid exploitation, clerical entitlement, or exclusion of disabled participants.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The unit directs gifts toward mutual service and God's glory.

interpretive_notes.note: Fiery trial may describe intensified local hostility, legal pressure, or metaphorically refining suffering; it does not by itself prove Nero's fire, Domitianic policy, or Trajanic procedure.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The phrase lacks a named event.

interpretive_notes.note: Suffering with Christ is consolation and identity formation, not permission for suffering glorification, victim blaming, trauma romanticization, self-harm, or keeping people in danger.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The passage distinguishes faithful endurance from wrongdoing and does not command preventable harm.

interpretive_notes.note: Judgment beginning with God's household may denote purifying ordeal, eschatological assessment, or another scriptural pattern; it does not authorize leaders to terrorize, purge, or publicly shame communities.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Divine judgment rhetoric is not delegated coercive power.

interpretive_notes.note: Elders are constrained by willingness, non-greed, non-domination, and exemplary conduct; shepherd language therefore cannot authorize clericalism, authoritarian leadership, financial abuse, or concealment.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The passage explicitly rejects domination.

interpretive_notes.note: Younger people are told to submit to elders and all to clothe themselves in humility; later age grades and offices should not erase reciprocal humility, accountability, or protection from abuse.
interpretive_notes.rationale: The sequence broadens humility beyond one subordinated group.

interpretive_notes.note: Casting anxiety on God offers care within distress; it must not shame anxiety disorders, replace mental-health treatment, demand emotional suppression, or blame sufferers when symptoms persist.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Spiritual consolation and evidence-based care are compatible.

interpretive_notes.note: The roaring-lion adversary is a vivid simile for threat; it cannot justify conspiracy theories, scapegoating, unsafe exorcism, or treating political and religious opponents as subhuman agents of Satan.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Vigilance and resistance do not license dehumanization.

interpretive_notes.note: Application must reject antisemitism, supersessionism, xenophobia, ethnic nationalism, colonial settlement, slavery apologetics, trafficking, worker exploitation, misogyny, anti-LGBTQ coercion, forced conversion, religious violence, prosperity extraction, and ecological neglect.
interpretive_notes.rationale: Modern reception must protect human dignity, consent, justice, and creation rather than baptize domination.

canonical_story.phase: Messiah communities in the Roman world
canonical_story.role: Forms dispersed assemblies for holy, hopeful, non-dominating witness amid social hostility.

hermeneutical_lens.immediate_literary_context: Read each disputed command inside its paragraph, especially the counterweights of freedom, universal honor, gentleness, mutual humility, non-domination, and divine care.
hermeneutical_lens.book_context: The opening identity and hope, central public and household conduct, and closing fiery-trial and elder exhortations form the primary horizon.
hermeneutical_lens.canonical_context: Trace Torah, Psalms, Prophets, Noah, Messiah, and apostolic-letter comparisons without erasing distinct rhetoric or Jewish scripture.
hermeneutical_lens.covenant_context: Treat election, holiness, people, priesthood, and mercy without supersessionism or ethnic nationalism.
hermeneutical_lens.historical_context: Keep authorship, Silvanus's role, date, Babylon, audience demographics, provincial route, and persecution scale qualified.
hermeneutical_lens.ancient_near_east_context: Use Hebrew Bible traditions as antecedents while avoiding a chronologically false ancient Near Eastern setting for First Peter.
hermeneutical_lens.second_temple_jewish_context: Compare election, diaspora, temple, spirit, Noah, apocalyptic, and scriptural traditions without inventing one sectarian source.
hermeneutical_lens.original_audience: Five provinces and the diaspora-sojourner address are explicit; exact cities, ethnicity, legal status, and organization are not.
hermeneutical_lens.genre: Letter combining blessing, paraenesis, scriptural catenae, household discourse, suffering rhetoric, baptismal language, and apocalyptic consolation.
intertextual_connections: Genesis 6-9 and Second Temple Noah traditions
Proverbs on humility and covering offense
Pauline household, suffering, and gift discourse
hermeneutical_lens.messianic_christological_trajectory: Jesus Christ's resurrection grounds hope; his blood frames ransom; his rejected and chosen stone identity forms the community; his unjust suffering is example and sin-bearing; his resurrection and exaltation ground baptismal and cosmic hope.
major_interpretive_views: Direct Petrine authorship, Petrine authorship through Silvanus, collaborative production, or post-Petrine pseudepigraphy
Babylon as Rome, literal Babylon, or another symbolic location
Predominantly gentile, predominantly Jewish, or mixed recipients
Localized social hostility, legal pressure, or more organized persecution
Fallen angels, human dead, or other beings as the spirits in prison
Sacramental, covenantal, symbolic, or faith-response readings of baptism
Historical accommodation, transformed patriarchy, or enduring norm in household exhortations
hermeneutical_lens.historical_interpretation: Early reception strongly favored apostolic Peter and Roman Babylon; later interpretation developed doctrines of descent, baptism, atonement, priesthood, and church order, while modern scholarship intensified social-historical, postcolonial, feminist, slavery, trauma, and anti-supersessionist critique.
hermeneutical_lens.authorial_intent: The received rhetoric aims to form dispersed addressees as hopeful, holy, mutually serving communities whose public conduct, nonretaliation, truthful witness, accountable leadership, and trust in God endure hostility; the historical author's identity remains disputed.
typological_connections: Noah's deliverance through water and baptismal antitype
Israel's priestly and holy calling applied to the addressees
Zion's rejected and chosen stone centered on Messiah
suffering righteous and servant imagery applied to Christ and community
hermeneutical_lens.christological_significance: Christ's suffering, death, resurrection, exaltation, ransom, sin-bearing, shepherding, and coming glory organize identity and hope; the difficult spirits and descent traditions require explicit qualification.
modern_application_principles: Build hopeful belonging for displaced and marginalized people without romanticizing precarity.
Practice public integrity while resisting coercive state, household, labor, and religious power.
Center the safety and testimony of enslaved, abused, and subordinated people when receiving household texts.
Use gifts through accountable, accessible, non-exploitative mutual service.
Require leaders to reject domination, greed, secrecy, and retaliation.
Join spiritual consolation with medical, mental-health, legal, and safeguarding care.
common_misinterpretations: The letter explicitly says Peter personally composed polished Greek from Rome during Nero's persecution.
Diaspora proves one ethnicity, legal status, or metaphorical meaning.
Royal priesthood means God rejected Jewish people or authorized a Christian nation-state.
Submission requires obedience to unjust rulers, enslavers, or abusive spouses.
Christ's suffering commands victims to remain in preventable harm.
Spirits in prison supplies a complete geography of the afterlife.
Baptism works magically or can be coerced.
Love covering sins requires institutional concealment.
